opus-5.5.text:
So the way we think about it, Scouts is really the first expression of a much bigger idea. The core insight is that a lot of what people do on the web is repetitive monitoring: checking for something, waiting for it to change, and then acting on it. Is there a new apartment listing in my neighborhood? Did a paper come out on a topic I care about? Did the price of something drop? Today you either do that manually over and over or you just give up. A Scout is an agent that does that watching for you, continuously, and tells you when something worth your attention shows up.

Starting there was deliberate. Monitoring is a workflow where the agent can be really useful without having to be perfect. It's mostly reading and synthesizing, not taking irreversible actions on your behalf. So it's a good place to build trust and to learn how people actually want to delegate to agents, what level of detail they want, how often they want to be pinged, how they phrase what they care about.

But the underlying machinery is general. To do a Scout well, you need an agent that can navigate the web, understand pages, keep state over time, reason about what's new versus what's noise, and communicate with the user in a natural way. Those are exactly the building blocks you need for a lot of other workflows. Once you have that, you can extend from "watch and notify" to "watch and summarize," to "watch and draft something," and eventually to "watch and act," like filling out a form, booking something, or kicking off a downstream task, with the user in the loop as much as they want.

So I see it as a ladder. We start with the part of the web that's about keeping up with things, get really good at that, earn people's trust, and then gradually take on more of the workflow. The long-term vision is that you have agents working in the background on your behalf across the web, and Scouts is the most natural, lowest-friction entry point into that world.

r001.rationale: It describes Scouts as continuously monitoring the web and gives varied applications: apartment listings, papers, and prices.

r002.rationale: It outlines a gradual expansion from watching and notifying to summarizing, drafting, and taking actions across more of a workflow.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so when we started Yutori, the thing we kept coming back to was this gap between what people say they want from an assistant and what the technology could reliably deliver. Everyone has a mental picture of the agent that just handles things for you. But if you tried to build that top-down, the general-purpose "do anything on the web" agent, you ended up with something that was impressive in demos and frustrating in daily use. It would get seventy percent of the way through a task and then fall over, and a seventy percent success rate on something that matters to you is kind of worse than nothing, because now you have to check everything.

So Scouts was us picking a wedge deliberately. The idea is really simple. You tell a Scout what you care about, in natural language, and it goes and watches the web for you. Monitor this apartment listing site for a two-bedroom under a certain price. Tell me when this conference announces its speakers. Watch for changes on a competitor's pricing page. Let me know when a specific sneaker comes back in stock. And it just keeps doing that, continuously, and surfaces what's relevant when it's relevant.

What I like about monitoring as a starting point is a few things. One, it's a genuine need. People are already doing this manually, badly, by refreshing tabs or setting up brittle Google Alerts. Two, the failure modes are forgiving. If a Scout checks a page and something's ambiguous, it can wait and check again. It's not booking a flight in your name. The cost of a mistake is low, and the cost of being right repeatedly is very high in terms of trust. And three, it's inherently long-running and personal. The agent accumulates context about what you care about. That's really different from the one-shot, chat-and-forget interaction that most people have had with AI so far.

And that last point is where the broader platform comes in. Once you've built the infrastructure for an agent that can navigate arbitrary websites, understand what's on them, remember what it saw last time, and act on a schedule or on triggers, you've actually built most of what you need for a lot of other workflows. Monitoring is "look and tell me." The next step is "look and, if this condition is met, do this thing." Fill out this form. Add this to my cart. Draft the email. Those are the same underlying capabilities, with the action surface expanded and the user in the loop at the right moments.

So we think of Scouts less as a product and more as the first thing people can reliably delegate. It's how we earn the right to be trusted with more. And honestly, it's also how we learn. Every Scout that runs is teaching us where the web is hard for agents, where sites are adversarial or inconsistent, where our models get confused. That data is what makes the general platform possible. I'd much rather get there bottom-up, from something that works today, than promise the moon and have people bounce off.

r001.rationale: The response frames Scouts as focused on continuously monitoring the web and gives examples across apartments, conferences, competitor pricing, and product availability.

r002.rationale: It describes building from monitoring toward conditional actions such as filling forms, adding items to a cart, and drafting emails, expanding the workflows users can delegate.

astra-6.text:
I think of Scouts as a concrete starting point for a broader idea: you should be able to describe what you want done on the web and have a system do that work for you. With Scouts, the workflow is about checking for something, doing that repeatedly, and letting you know when there’s something worth your attention.

That gives us a useful setting to work through some of the harder questions. Can the system understand what you care about? Can it find the relevant information? Can it distinguish a meaningful change from noise? And can it do that reliably over time?

Those capabilities can support other workflows, too. You can imagine moving from finding information to synthesizing it, comparing options, and eventually taking an action. But each step introduces new questions about permissions and when to bring the user back into the loop. So I see Scouts as a way to make one workflow useful, learn from how people use it, and build toward that broader platform.

r001.rationale: The response describes Scouts monitoring for changes and extending into other workflows, but it does not distinguish that monitoring capability from the broad range of domains where it could be applied.

r002.rationale: It describes building outward from finding information to synthesizing, comparing options, and eventually taking action, presenting these as steps toward a broader platform.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of Scouts as a very concrete starting point: you tell the system what you care about, and it goes out on the web, checks for changes, and brings back what’s relevant to you. That’s useful on its own, but it also gives us a way to learn what it takes for an agent to do reliable work over time.

The broader opportunity is that a lot of web workflows share those same pieces. You need to understand someone’s intent, find the right information, keep track of context, and decide what to do next. Sometimes the output is simply an update. Sometimes you want the system to take another step, with your approval.

So I see Scouts as a starting point for building those capabilities around a well-defined experience. As we learn where people find value and where they want more control, we can expand into richer workflows. The goal is for people to describe what they want accomplished without having to specify every click along the way.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts Scouts’ web monitoring with broader web workflows, but does not clearly say the monitoring capability can apply across a broad range of domains.

r002.rationale: It describes learning from the initial experience and expanding into richer workflows, including taking additional steps, so Scouts handles more of what users want accomplished over time.
